https://www.dw.com/en/turkish-somali-for.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Jd4B Puntland Maritime Police Forces PMPF patrol against the pirate attacks off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024] Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO Advertisement Turkey ’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia ’s government said on Saturday. "During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship." The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries. The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey." According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national. Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year. At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen. Maritime police patrol to ward off piracy off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024] Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu/picture alliance These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somalia in the 2000s . It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping. The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea. In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping. https://www.politico.eu/article/chatgpt-.text: La décision de l’UE de réglementer ChatGPT en le considérant comme un moteur de recherche paraîtra logique à ceux qui l’utilisent comme tel. Mais qu’en est-il si vous l’utilisez comme un ami ? Ou comme un thérapeute ? Ou encore pour discuter des prochaines élections ? Ce sont là quelques-unes des nombreuses nouvelles questions que l’avènement de l’IA générative soulève pour les régulateurs européens — qui, selon les experts, n’ont pas encore trouvé de réponses satisfaisantes. Lundi, l’exécutif européen a classé ChatGPT parmi les “très grands moteurs de recherche en ligne” au titre du règlement sur les services numériques (DSA), lui imposant ainsi une série d’obligations en matière de transparence et d’atténuation des risques similaires à celles auxquelles sont soumis les leaders traditionnels du secteur, tels que Google et Bing (de Microsoft), qui comptent plus de 45 millions d’utilisateurs mensuels. La société mère de ChatGPT, OpenAI, s’expose à des amendes pouvant atteindre 6% de son chiffre d’affaires mondial annuel si elle ne respecte pas ces règles. Advertisement Advertisement Toutefois, cette catégorisation est restrictive et ne s’applique qu’aux parties de l’outil qui font office de moteur de recherche, ce qui signifie que les conversations dans lesquelles le chatbot apporte sa propre contribution ne semblent pas être concernées. En application du DSA, la Commission aurait pu choisir de classer ChatGPT dans la catégorie des “très grandes plateformes en ligne”, qui s’applique généralement aux réseaux sociaux et aux plateformes d’e-commerce et qui impose des obligations différentes. Pourtant, aucune de ces deux catégories ne reflète l’éventail des utilisations possibles des chatbots . “ChatGPT est bien plus qu’un simple moteur de recherche, et il existe également des risques liés au chatbot lui-même qui échappent aux obligations les plus strictes [du règlement]”, a pointé Christel Schaldemose, députée européenne socialiste danoise, qui figurait parmi les principaux négociateurs de cette législation. La députée européenne Christel Schaldemose a souligné les risques pour les enfants. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images Elle a mis en avant les risques pour les enfants, “comme la dépendance affective et la conception manipulatrice ou addictive”, et a exhorté la Commission à préciser dans quelle mesure ces risques sont pris en compte par la réglementation en vigueur. ChatGPT et ses concurrents font l’objet d’une polémique mondiale, car ils auraient contribué aux suicides tragiques d’adolescents, notamment celui d’Adam Raine, un jeune Californien de 16 ans, dont les parents ont engagé des poursuites judiciaires contre l’entreprise. Les cas d’utilisation de chatbots basés sur l’IA pour une thérapie ou pour avoir de la compagnie ne sont pas marginaux : selon une étude récente menée par le secteur des assurances, pas moins de 60% des adultes dans le monde les utilisent à des fins thérapeutiques . Advertisement Advertisement Un espace hybride La législation actuelle sur les services numériques, adoptée en 2022, n’avait pas prévu l’essor des chatbots . João Pedro Quintais, maître de conférences en droit à l’université d’Amsterdam, décrit ChatGPT comme une technologie “hybride” qui combine les fonctions d’un moteur de recherche et d’une plateforme en ligne, ainsi que d’autres fonctions plus proches de celles d’un éditeur de ses propres contenus. La qualification de “moteur de recherche” pourrait limiter la capacité de la Commission à contrôler la manière dont ChatGPT gère les risques liés non seulement à la santé mentale des adolescents, mais aussi à l’intégrité des élections ou aux contenus illicites. Demander à ChatGPT de citer les noms des candidats à une élection locale devrait désormais relever du champ d’application du DSA. En revanche, une conversation entre un utilisateur et un chatbot sur le choix du candidat pour lequel voter, au cours de laquelle des informations erronées pourraient être diffusées, pourrait ne pas être concernée. Il a fallu un peu moins d’un an à la Commission pour finaliser la classification de ce chatbot , ses équipes s’étant heurtées à des difficultés pour déterminer dans quelle catégorie le classer. Selon les experts, sans avoir consulté le texte intégral actant cette classification annoncée cette semaine, il est difficile de savoir exactement quelles seront les obligations d’OpenAI. La qualification de “plateforme” aurait imposé à OpenAI des obligations supplémentaires en matière de modération des contenus au titre du règlement sur les services numériques, mais elle aurait aussi permis à l’entreprise d’échapper à une part importante de ses responsabilités. Le DSA, comme d’autres législations dans le monde relatives aux plateformes, s’articule autour du principe du “ safe harbor ”, en vertu duquel les entreprises ne sont pas responsables des contenus présents sur leurs plateformes, ceux-ci étant mis en ligne par les utilisateurs. Mais l’avènement des chatbots soulève la question de savoir si une conversation entre une personne et une machine peut être considérée comme un “contenu généré par les utilisateurs”. Modèles et risques Si l’attention portée par les autorités de régulation à ChatGPT en tant qu’application grand public est récente, la Commission surveille de près les modèles d’intelligence artificielle qui la sous-tendent via son règlement sur l’IA ( AI Act ). Advertisement Advertisement OpenAI, la société mère de ChatGPT, ainsi que des entreprises telles qu’Anthropic et Gemini (de Google) développent ce que l’on appelle des modèles d’IA à usage général, capables d’effectuer une grande variété de tâches pouvant présenter des “risques systémiques potentiels”. Depuis août dernier, au titre de l’ AI Act , ces entreprises ont l’obligation d’“évaluer et d’atténuer” les risques que présentent ces modèles. La Commission a commencé à faire appliquer cette législation fin août, lorsqu’elle a cuisiné une série d’entreprises spécialisées dans l’IA sur leurs procédures de sécurité. Auparavant, un groupe d’experts avait identifié quatre risques : la mise au point d’armes nucléaires ou biologiques, la perte de contrôle sur les modèles, des modèles d’IA hors de contrôle qui commencent à faire du piratage, ou encore des modèles se livrant à des manipulations à grande échelle. Illustration d’un ami virtuel sur l’écran d’un iPhone. | Olivier Douliery/AFP via Getty Images Mais aussi effrayants soient-ils, ces risques systémiques ne prennent pas en compte toute une série de problèmes potentiels, tant pour les utilisateurs que pour la société dans son ensemble. “[Ces orientations] sont davantage axées sur ce qu’on appelle les risques existentiels que sur les risques pesant sur les droits fondamentaux”, a soulevé Daniel Leufer, responsable des politiques en matière de technologies émergentes chez AccessNow. Il a fait valoir qu’avec la classification de ChatGPT au titre du DSA, il y a une chance “d’entrer dans les détails des choix de conception et de considérer ChatGPT davantage pour ce qu’il est réellement, à savoir un produit”. Advertisement Advertisement L’intelligence artificielle ayant eu un impact aussi rapide et profond, la réglementation en la matière est encore en cours d’élaboration. Le député européen social-démocrate italien Brando Benifei, qui mène les travaux sur les questions l’intelligence artificielle au Parlement, a défendu l’approche européenne qui distingue la supervision des applications de celle des modèles d’IA, affirmant que ces deux cadres réglementaires peuvent se “compléter puissamment”. Brando Benifei a toutefois reconnu qu’une supervision dans le cadre du DSA était “absolument nécessaire” pour protéger les personnes qui utilisent vraiment les outils d’IA, citant comme exemple concret les “dépendances dangereuses en matière de santé mentale” que certaines personnes développent à l’égard des chatbots compagnons. “L’examen s’étend désormais du modèle sous-jacent à la manière dont ces services sont concrètement conçus et déployés.” Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-envoys-witkoff-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Lhl5 The US envoys met Zelenskyy after talking to Putin in Moscow Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS Advertisement US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made their first official visit to Ukraine on Sunday as part of fresh efforts toward peace with Russia . As Ukraine's airspace remains closed due to the conflict, the pair arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland, having spent more than three hours in talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier. Putin had declared a three-day ceasefire to ensure the envoys' safety. Ukraine peace push? Trump envoys hold talks with Kremlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Zelenskyy: Ukraine's peace proposals are ready Ahead of the visit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media that Kyiv is ready for a “constructive” discussion with its US counterparts. “We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer," he wrote. "Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared.” Reuters news agency reported that national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France and Germany were also in Kyiv for talks with the US envoys, citing a source familiar with the matter. Momentum by US President Donald Trump to end the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict has stalled in recent months after talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January failed to produce a result. Ukraine's Budanov expects war to continue for many months Despite hopes of a breakthrough with the Russian leader on Saturday, there were no announcements after the meeting. Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow talks as constructive, frank, and useful but didn’t discuss specific outcomes. Ushakov said the talks also focused on economic issues and potentially large Russia-US projects. During previous talks, negotiators have struggled to bring both sides together on a range of key issues, including the future of the industrial Donbas region of eastern Ukraine. The US and Russia have been discussing tie-ins for months to try and end the war Image: Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/AP Photo/picture alliance For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and Washington are crucial to deterring Russia ​from further aggression. Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, told the New York Times last weekend that he did not expect the fighting to end before spring 2027. He also predicted further Russian strategic air strikes on Ukraine this winter. The war has escalated in recent months, with Putin seeking the complete conquest of Dombas and Russian drones targeting the Ukrainian capital. Meanwhile, Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russia's energy sector. It has also targeted online retailers deep inside Russia to try and bring the war home to the public. BuraÄo / A. BuraÄo asmeninio archyvo nuotr. A large-format painting by Lithuanian landscape master and watercolourist Jonas BuraÄas, Lithuaniaâs Gateway to the Seas, has been brought back to life. The painting was taken to Germany by the Nazis in July 1944 and subsequently disappeared. âThe story of the canvas being stolen is, I would say, a typical example of Nazi behaviour in the occupied territories,â said Romualdas BeniuÅ¡is, a historian. He worked together with Antanas BuraÄas, son of the late painter, as well as painter Rodionas Petrovas and Memelio Miesto real estate developers in the port city of KlaipÄda to bring the painting back to life. According to BeniuÅ¡is, returning works of art to their rightful owners is a difficult problem to solve. Lithuanian institutions can point to only a handful of successful cases in this area. Unfortunately, BuraÄasâ painting is not among them. In 1938, BuraÄas won a competition organised by the KlaipÄda Chamber of Commerce and Industry to depict Lithuaniaâs maritime gateway to the world. The work was intended as a gift to the newly established Kaunas Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Crafts, designed by architect Vytautas Landsbergis-Å½emkalnis. Painter and watercolourist BuraÄas (1898â1977) was born in Sidariai, in the RadviliÅ¡kis area in northern Lithuania. He graduated from the Kaunas Art School and furthered his studies in Paris, Berlin and Riga. He became known for his depictions of Lithuaniaâs landscapes, towns, hillforts and architectural monuments, painted in a realistic style influenced by Impressionism and Pointillism. From 1945 to 1951, he taught at the Kaunas Art School and the Kaunas Institute of Applied and Decorative Arts. From 1950, he devoted himself mainly to his creative work, leaving behind a significant collection of images of Lithuaniaâs landscapes and cultural heritage. The renowned landscape painter worked âfrom natureâ. During summers spent on the coast, he produced numerous works and watercolours. Jonas BuraÄas | Antanas BuraÄas' personal archives âIt seems the dimensions of the painting had been agreed in advance with the architect, and a place for it to be displayed had also been designated in the building. The canvas, approximately 2 metres high and 4 metres long, was the first of this size that BuraÄas had painted,â BeniuÅ¡is says. BuraÄas took up residence at a local guesthouse and got to work. After moving to SmiltynÄ, he made sketches and took photographs. This is documented in archival material left to his son, Antanas BuraÄas. A prize of 5,000 litas was awarded for the work, with BuraÄas receiving 3,500. The organisers used the remaining money to cover the artistâs accommodation costs. According to BeniuÅ¡is, a photograph of the painting appeared in the KlaipÄda newspaper Vakarai on September 16, 1938. âBuraÄas depicted a panorama of KlaipÄdaâs port and city as seen from SmiltynÄ. Some of the landmarks no longer survive. For example, St Johnâs Church, which had a 75-metre-high tower with a clock. The artist painted the Reformed and Laukininkai churches, the LietÅ«kis warehouses and the Pilotsâ Tower,â the local historian says. In February 1939, the Kaunas Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Crafts celebrated the opening of its new premises. BuraÄasâ monumental work became a prominent part of the chamberâs interior. After the Soviet occupation, the chamber was nationalised. âBuraÄasâs canvas was supposed to be transferred to the M K Äiurlionis Art Gallery, but for some reason it never reached the gallery,â BeniuÅ¡is says. After the Nazis occupied Lithuania, the official governor of the territory, Theodor Adrian von Renteln, set up his headquarters in the Chamber of Commerce building, while taking up residence in the house of industrialist Jonas Vailokaitis, a signatory of Lithuaniaâs February 16 Act of Independence, in VienybÄs Square. âApparently, the ânewcomersâ liked BuraÄasâs canvas depicting KlaipÄdaâs port and city â the Nazis considered it their own. So when they had to retreat in 1944, the painting was taken away along with other property looted in Lithuania,â the local historian says. According to him, evidence of the workâs whereabouts in Frankfurt am Main was later recorded in several documents, including the 1981 catalogue Jonas BuraÄasâ Paintings and a book by Lithuanian Ã©migrÃ© journalist and local historian Bronius Kviklys. The finished painting, 1938. | R. BeniuÅ¡is personal archives State showed no interest The artistâs son, Antanas BuraÄas, tells LRT.lt that he became interested in the paintingâs history after finding a description by art collector Vladas Å½ukas in his fatherâs archive. The artist had told Å½ukas that he had personally seen German soldiers in 1944 cut the canvas from its frame, roll it up and load it onto a lorry parked in the courtyard of the Chamber of Commerce. âIt was later discovered that the theft had been carried out on the orders of Renteln, the general commissioner of Ostland,â the artistâs son adds. In 1989, Antanas BuraÄas visited Chicago, where he spoke to fellow Lithuanians about the SÄ jÅ«dis movement and the aspirations of the Lithuanian people. There he met Bronius Kviklys, a prominent Lithuanian Ã©migrÃ© journalist, ethnographer and historian. Kviklys told his visitor that, after the war, while living in a displaced persons (DP) camp, he had seen the painting Lithuaniaâs Gateway to the Seas in a museum in Frankfurt am Main. Antanas says he was more interested at the time in Kviklysâ other accounts and was focused on the affairs of Lithuania undergoing a national revival, so he did not remember the name of the museum. Kviklys died a year later. When interest in the fate of the painting resurfaced in recent years, Antanas contacted Germanyâs commission dealing with property confiscated by the Nazis. The commission replied that it would be happy to help search for the work, but that the artistâs son would have to provide proof of ownership. âThe owner was effectively the Kaunas Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Crafts. After 1940, I believe its property was nationalised by the Soviets and should have become state property. During the war, my father asked Paulius GalaunÄ [director of the M K Äiurlionis Art Gallery] to shelter the canvas somewhere. âBut the work was very inconvenient because of its size, so it was left without being hidden. I believe the current successor in title is the Lithuanian state, and the Culture Ministry should represent its interests,â Antanas BuraÄas says. He and BeniuÅ¡is approached the ministry, but heard no more about anyone taking decisive action. Rodionas Petrovas standing next to his rendition of the missing painting. | D. Rimeikoas âHouston, we have a problemâ âAs you know, I like getting involved in all sorts of adventures. And when an adventure begins... âHouston, we have a problem!â The harsh reality stares you in the face,â says painter Rodionas Petrovas, who recreated BuraÄasâs painting. He is neither a copyist nor a landscape painter nor a restorer â that is not his field. However, he realised that there might not be another professional in KlaipÄda capable of recreating the painting with the necessary technical skill. So he accepted the offer. Besides, Petrovas had experience working with architecture, which is also one of the themes of his work. According to the artist, the hardest part was that only two black-and-white photographs of BuraÄasâ painting survive. It is very difficult to make out specific details in them. Petrovas set out to find images of all the buildings depicted in the painting. In search of high-quality panoramic photographs, he visited museums, libraries and archives. He found KÄstutis Demereckasâs book, KlaipÄda in Old Postcards, particularly helpful. It was also necessary to understand the contrast between the tones in the original. âThen you can work out what colours the artist used,â Petrovas says. According to him, BuraÄas used vivid colours when he painted the work in the late 1930s. Petrovas himself opted for a more muted palette. âI thought that, since I was partly creating a historical interpretation, I could allow myself to tone down the colours so that it would look like a work that has stood the test of time,â he says. Petrovas has two theories to explain the mystery surrounding the paintingâs high-altitude perspective. According to one, the landscape painter viewed the panorama of KlaipÄda from the Kurhaus, at the time the tallest building in SmiltynÄ, and gradually widened his field of view in his sketches. âThat is no problem for a professional,â he says. His other, âconspiratorialâ, theory is linked to the fact that an airship flew to KlaipÄda during the interwar period. BuraÄas may have used photographs taken from the airship. In 2027, it will be 50 years since BuraÄasâ death, and the following year will mark 130 years since his birth. Is his son considering how these anniversaries might be commemorated? âIt is very gratifying that, just before these anniversaries, there has suddenly been some excitement about the great painting and its rediscovery. As a panorama, it has turned out to be not bad at all and has deserved this attention. I am very pleased about that,â says Antanas. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Amnesty International called the verdict against Lina Attalah 'a crushing blow to press freedom' (file photo) By David Gritten Published 1 hour ago The editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr has been taken into custody after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure, her lawyers say. Lina Attalah will be held until she pays the fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; Â£40,100) also handed down by the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court. It was the maximum possible penalty for the charge, which she had rejected. The human rights group Amnesty International said the verdict represented "a crushing blow to press freedom". It comes only weeks after six journalists working for the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ). President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has overseen what human rights groups say is an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since he led the military's overthrow of his predecessor, Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Morsi, in 2013. Tens of thousands of people have been detained, mainly Brotherhood officials and supporters but also leading secular and liberal activists, media workers and academics. Egyptian journalists from fact-checking website facing terrorism charges Published 6 October AI 'SpongeBob' parody of problems in Egypt draws scrutiny of authorities Published 15 September TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case Published 6 September The CPJ said Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt and that it had long faced pressure from authorities over its journalism. The site had repeatedly sought an operating licence from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) since a new media law was passed in 2018, but that its applications were either rejected or left unanswered, the media watchdog added. Amnesty International said Lina Attalah had also faced "years of harassment and intimidation", including six criminal investigations over Mada Masr's reporting. Last week, prosecutors summoned her for questioning over allegations of publishing "false news" and operating a website without a licence. Mada Masr's lawyer said the investigation included a recent report that the website had published about a wave of protests in prisons across the country, as well as a letter from the SMRC regarding its legal status. Attalah was released on bail and later referred to trial before the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court on the charge of operating a website without a licence. During Tuesday's hearing, Judge Mohammed Mubarak ordered the courtroom to be cleared of everyone except Attalah, her eight-person defence team, and Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), an independent human rights group. Bahgat told AFP news agency that security personnel then filed in before the judge announced that the court was denying several procedural requests made by the defence and appointing its own lawyer for Attalah. "In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," he said. "Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes. "In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer - who had not uttered a single word - and entered them into the official record," he added. The judge then announced the fine for Attalah and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before she was detained, according to Bahgat. Amnesty International warned that the court's verdict marked "a dark day for independent journalism" in Egypt and demanded that it be overturned. "This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices," said the group's senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed. "Lina Attalah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job." CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah said: "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting."
